Validation

/val-ih-DAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Validation means the act of confirming that something is true, accurate, or justified; official confirmation or approval

Validation means the act of confirming that something is true, accurate, or justified; official confirmation or approval

Worked Example

The inspector's report gave the residents' complaints official <strong style="color:var(--accent);">validation</strong>: the elevator really had been skipping floors for months.

The report confirms that the complaints were true and justified — an outside authority verifying the residents were right — which is exactly what validation provides.

How Strong Is It? — acknowledgment → validation → certification

acknowledgment vs. validation

acknowledgment vs. validation: Acknowledgment is milder than validation — acknowledging a complaint just notes that it exists, while validation confirms the complaint is actually justified.

certification vs. validation

certification vs. validation: Certification is stronger than validation — it adds a formal, official seal, like an agency certifying that a product meets every published standard.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — valid-

Root — valid-: strong, effective (Latin validus, from valere, to be strong or to be worth)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: the action or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Valid- ('strong') plus -ation ('the act of') gives the literal sense 'the act of making or declaring something strong' — validation confirms that a claim stands up under weight.

Use the root in a new word: prevail

Use the root in a new word: prevail: Despite two early setbacks, the smaller robotics team managed to prevail in the final round — literally proving itself the stronger.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral; technical and emotional senses

Validation wears two hats. The official flavor confirms accuracy or approval: validation of a parking ticket, of test results, of a passport. The emotional flavor is the feeling that your experience has been recognized as real and reasonable ('her friends' support gave her validation'). Both senses share one core idea: confirmation that something stands up. Common patterns: 'validation of a claim,' 'validation for one's efforts.'
